entry: Diagram showing all possible logical relations between a collection of sets. In a Venn diagram, sets are shown as regions inside overlapping closed curves, usually [[Circle|circles]], and each point inside a curve represents an element of that set. The area where two curves overlap shows the elements common to both sets, their [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]], and the combined area is their [[Union (set theory)|union]]. Earlier proposals include Christian Weise's of 1712 and Leonhard Euler's of 1768, but John Venn introduced the form in 1880 and popularized it in *Symbolic Logic* (1881). Because every possible overlap is drawn, Venn diagrams are a special case of Euler diagrams, which need not show all relations. They are used to teach [[Set theory|elementary set theory]] and to illustrate relationships in [[Probability|probability]], [[Logic|logic]], [[Statistics|statistics]] and [[Computer science|computer science]].

Toxin produced by an animal and actively delivered to another animal through a [[Wound|wound]], usually by a bite, sting or other penetrative action. Venoms are injected through specialized structures such as fangs or stingers, a process called envenomation, and differ from [[Poison|poisons]], which are passively ingested, inhaled or absorbed through the skin. Venom has evolved independently at least 104 times across eight phyla, among predators and prey and in both [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] and [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], on land and in water. Venoms kill through at least four major classes of toxin: necrotoxins and cytotoxins, which kill cells; neurotoxins, which affect nervous systems; myotoxins, which damage muscles; and hemotoxins, which disrupt blood clotting. Venomous animals cause tens of thousands of human deaths each year. Toxins from venom are used to treat conditions including thrombosis, [[Arthritis|arthritis]] and some [[Cancer|cancers]].

Ancient Greek marble statue, probably of [[Aphrodite|Aphrodite]], displayed in the [[Louvre|Louvre]] in Paris. The modern consensus dates it to the [[Hellenistic period|Hellenistic period]], most likely the 2nd century BC, perhaps between 160 and 110 BC. It was discovered on the Greek island of Milos in 1820 and has been displayed at the Louvre since 1821. Carved from Parian marble, the statue stands over 2 metres (6 ft 7 in) high and has lost both arms. A now-lost inscription found nearby is the basis for attributing it to Alexandros of Antioch on the Maeander, but the name is uncertain and its connection to the statue is disputed. Classical scholars first dated it to the early 4th century BC, but in the late 19th century it was reinterpreted as Hellenistic. It became a cornerstone of the Louvre's collection after the [[Napoleonic Wars|Napoleonic Wars]], and copies spread its fame. It inspired more than 70 poems and influenced 19th-century art and the Surrealist movement.

[[Carnivorous plant|Carnivorous plant]] species native to wetlands of [[North Carolina|North Carolina]] and [[South Carolina|South Carolina]]. It is the only species in its genus. Its leaf tips form snap traps that catch mainly [[Insect|insects]] and [[Arachnid|arachnids]]. Trigger hairs on the traps must be touched twice within about twenty seconds for the trap to close, and digestion begins only after five more stimuli, so the plant avoids wasting energy on nonfood objects. The hairs also sense heat, so a forest fire can close them. Its wild population has declined rapidly, and in 2017 it was under review under the Endangered Species Act.

Roman goddess whose functions encompassed love, beauty, desire, sex, [[Fertility|fertility]], prosperity and victory. In [[Roman mythology|Roman mythology]], she was the ancestor of the Roman people through her son Aeneas, who survived the fall of Troy and fled to Italy, and [[Julius Caesar|Julius Caesar]] claimed her as his own ancestor. Venus was central to many religious festivals and was revered under numerous cult titles. The Romans adapted the myths and iconography of the Greek [[Aphrodite|Aphrodite]] for [[Roman art|Roman art]] and [[Latin literature|Latin literature]]. In the later classical tradition of the West, she became one of the most widely referenced deities of Greco-Roman mythology as the embodiment of love and sexuality, and she is usually depicted nude. Her name is related to the Latin word *venus*, meaning 'love' or 'charm'.

Prehistoric figurine, 11.1 centimetres (4.4 in) tall, estimated to have been made c. 30,000 years ago. It was recovered on August 7, 1908, during an excavation of a [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]] site near Willendorf, a village in [[Austria|Lower Austria]]. The figure is carved from oolitic [[Limestone|limestone]] that is not local to the area and was tinted with [[Ochre|red ochre]]. It is in the Natural History Museum in [[Vienna|Vienna]]. The name Venus reflects speculation that the figure depicts a fertility goddess, a metaphor since such figurines predate the mythological [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]] by many thousands of years. Others suggest it may be a self-portrait. Evidence of the sculptor's intent is scant. Research published in 2022 indicates that the stone most likely came from northern Italy, near Lake Garda.

Port city and municipal seat on the [[Gulf of Mexico|Gulf of Mexico]] (pop., 2020: 537,952), in Veracruz state, [[Mexico|Mexico]]. It is Mexico's oldest, largest and historically most significant port. [[Hernán Cortés|Hernán Cortés]] founded the settlement on April 22, 1519, as Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz (True Cross), because he landed on Good Friday. In 1523 it became the first Spanish settlement on the American mainland to receive a coat of arms. During the colonial period the city was at times wealthier than the capital, Mexico City, and fortifications such as Fort San Juan de Ulúa were built against 17th-century pirates. France and the United States invaded the city in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and U.S. troops occupied it for seven months after the 1914 Tampico Affair. Petroleum dominated the state's economy for much of the 20th century, but the port has since become the principal port for most of Mexico's imports and exports, especially automobiles. Its culture blends indigenous, Spanish and Afro-Caribbean influences, most visible in its food and music.

Part of speech that generally conveys an action (bring, read, walk), an occurrence (happen, become) or a state of being (be, exist, stand). In many [[Language|languages]], verbs are inflected to encode tense, aspect, mood and voice, and they may agree with the person, gender or number of their subject or object. English has three tenses: present, past and future, the last expressed with the auxiliary verb *will* or *shall*. Verbs are usually classified by the number of arguments they take, and four basic types are distinguished: intransitive, transitive, ditransitive and double transitive. Some verbs have special grammatical roles, such as copular verbs like *be* and the auxiliaries *have* and *can*. [[Latin|Latin]] and the [[Romance languages|Romance languages]] inflect verbs for tense, aspect and mood and agree with the subject in person and number. The word *verb* comes from Latin *verbum*, meaning word or verb, and shares an Indo-European root with [[Word|word]].

[[Genus|Genus]] of about 150 species of annual and perennial herbaceous or semi-woody [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family Verbenaceae, also known as vervain. Most species are native to the Americas and Asia, but the type species, common vervain (*Verbena officinalis*), is native to Europe. Several species and hybrids are grown as ornamentals because they are drought-resistant and attract butterflies and hummingbirds. The Silver Anne and Sissinghurst hybrids have won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Verbena has long been used in herbalism and [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]], although there is no high-quality evidence for its effectiveness. It is one of 38 plants used in Bach flower remedies, a form of alternative medicine. The essential oil of common vervain, sold as Spanish verbena oil, has some commercial importance in herbalism. The plant was once called the tears of [[Isis|Isis]] in ancient Egypt.

Gallic chieftain of the Arverni who united most of [[Gaul|Gaul]] in a failed revolt against [[Rome|Rome]]. Exiled in early 52 BC for urging revolt, he returned with supporters, was proclaimed king and was elected to command a coalition of tribes against [[Julius Caesar|Julius Caesar]] in the [[Gallic Wars|Gallic Wars]]. He aimed to exhaust the Roman forces through scorched-earth tactics and harassment. After early successes, including a Roman defeat at Gergovia, he was forced to surrender at the Battle of Alesia in September 52 BC. He was held in Rome for six years and executed after Caesar's triumph. Most of what is known of him derives from Caesar's own account, which uses him to personify Celtic resistance. Largely overlooked in the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]], he was rediscovered in the 16th century, and from the 19th century he became a symbol of French national identity and of resistance to foreign domination.

Toxic red [[Pigment|pigment]] made by grinding the mineral [[Cinnabar|cinnabar]], a form of mercury sulfide. Vermilion is synonymous with red-orange, but it is not one hue: particle size produces shades from bright orange-red to a duller reddish purple. The Chinese probably made a synthetic version as early as the 4th century BC, and the Persian alchemist [[Jabir ibn Hayyan|Jabir ibn Hayyan]] described the process in the 9th century. A 17th-century Dutch method is still used today with essentially the same process. The pigment tends to darken, and like most mercury compounds it is toxic.

Landlocked state in the [[New England|New England]] region of the northeastern United States, bordered by [[Quebec|Quebec]] to the north. Its estimated population of 644,663 makes it the second-least populous state, and its capital, Montpelier, is the least populous U.S. state capital. An independent Vermont Republic was established in 1777, and it abolished [[Slavery|slavery]] before any other U.S. state. Vermont was admitted to the Union in 1791 as the 14th state. Its economy ranks last among states and territories by GDP, but it has the highest proportion of renewable electricity generation, at 99.9%, and it produces approximately 50% of the nation's maple syrup.

1958 American psychological thriller film directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock|Alfred Hitchcock]]. Based on the 1954 novel *D'entre les morts* by Boileau-Narcejac, it stars [[James Stewart|James Stewart]] as a former San Francisco police detective who retired after developing an extreme fear of heights. He is hired to follow the wife of an acquaintance from college, and the investigation of her strange behavior draws him into a troubled romance. Much of the film was shot on location in [[San Francisco|San Francisco]], and it was the first film to use the dolly zoom, an in-camera effect that distorts perspective to convey disorientation, often called the *Vertigo* effect. It received mixed reviews on release but later came to be considered Hitchcock's masterpiece. In 1989 the [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]] selected it for the United States National Film Registry, and in the 2012 *Sight & Sound* poll of critics it replaced *Citizen Kane* as the greatest film ever made, placing second in 2022.

Branch of [[Medicine|medicine]] concerned with the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of disease and injury in non-human [[Animal|animals]], both domesticated and wild. It is practiced by veterinarians, supported by paraveterinary workers such as veterinary nurses and technicians. Veterinary science helps human health by monitoring and controlling zoonotic diseases, supports food safety and [[Livestock|livestock]] health, and keeps pets healthy. Veterinarians are ethically obliged to look after animal welfare. Veterinary procedures date to the [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] (3400–3000 BC), shown by a trepanned cow skull, and the first surviving record is the Egyptian Papyrus of Kahun from the Twelfth Dynasty. The Indian treatise Shalihotra Samhita dates from the time of [[Ashoka|Ashoka]], and early efforts to regulate care focused on [[Horse|horses]]. The first veterinary school was founded in [[Lyon|Lyon]], France, by Claude Bourgelat, and its model drew on human medicine, natural history and comparative anatomy.

[[Sex toy|Sex toy]] that produces pleasurable stimulation through vibration. Most modern vibrators contain an electric device that pulsates or throbs, often using eccentric weights driven by a motor, though some use electromagnetic coils. They come in many shapes, including clitoral wands and bullets and [[Dildo|dildo]]-shaped models for vaginal, anal or oral use. Some modern vibrators synchronize their vibrations to music. Sex therapists recommend vibrators for women who have difficulty reaching [[Orgasm|orgasm]] through masturbation or intercourse.

French state headed by Marshal [[Philippe Pétain|Philippe Pétain]] from 1940 to 1944, during [[World War II|World War II]]. It was established after the German victory in the [[Battle of France|Battle of France]] and governed the unoccupied southern zone from Vichy while Germany occupied the north and west. It adopted a policy of collaboration with [[Nazi Germany|Nazi Germany]] and promoted [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] and an authoritarian program called *Révolution nationale*. After Allied landings in North Africa in November 1942, Germany occupied the rest of France, and at least 72,500 [[Jews|Jews]] deported from Vichy France were killed in [[Nazi concentration camps|Nazi concentration camps]].

Species of vetch in the pea and bean family [[Fabaceae|Fabaceae]], commonly called the broad bean, fava bean or faba bean. It is widely cultivated for human food and as a cover crop that prevents [[Erosion|erosion]] and fixes nitrogen in the soil. Varieties with smaller, harder seeds, called field beans, are fed to livestock. Some people have favism, a hemolytic reaction to broad beans linked to a metabolic disorder known as G6PDD. Otherwise the beans can be eaten raw or cooked once the outer seed coat is removed. Charred remains from [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] sites in [[Israel|Israel]]'s Lower Galilee suggest domestication may have begun as early as 8250 BC. The plant is hardy and tolerates saline and clay soils, though it prefers rich [[Loam|loams]]. Its diploid genome contains 13 GB of DNA and a predicted 34,221 protein-coding genes.

French [[Romanticism|Romantic]] writer, poet, playwright and politician. His best-known novels are *The Hunchback of Notre-Dame* (1831) and *Les Misérables* (1862), and his poetry includes *Les Contemplations* and *La Légende des siècles*. He was at the forefront of the Romantic movement in theatre with the plays *Cromwell* and *Hernani*. His works inspired the opera *Rigoletto* and the musicals *Les Misérables* and *Notre-Dame de Paris*. He produced more than 4,000 drawings and campaigned for the abolition of capital punishment and slavery. A committed royalist when young, he became a passionate supporter of republicanism and served in politics as both a deputy and a senator. His opposition to absolutism and his literary stature made him a national hero. His state funeral in the Panthéon in [[Paris|Paris]] was attended by over two million people, the largest in French history.

Capital of [[British Columbia|British Columbia]], Canada (pop., 2021: 91,867), on the southern tip of [[Vancouver Island|Vancouver Island]]. Named for [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]], it is one of the oldest cities in the [[Pacific Northwest|Pacific Northwest]], with British settlement beginning in 1843. Its landmarks include the Parliament Buildings, finished in 1897, and the Empress Hotel, opened in 1908. Its Chinatown is the second oldest in North America, after [[San Francisco|San Francisco]]. Known as the Garden City, it is a popular tourist destination, and technology is its largest revenue-generating private industry.

Waterfall on the [[Zambezi|Zambezi]] River, on the border between [[Zambia|Zambia]] and [[Zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]]. Known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, meaning the smoke that thunders, it is one of the world's largest waterfalls, with a width of 1,708 m (5,604 ft). Scottish missionary [[David Livingstone|David Livingstone]] first recorded viewing it on November 16, 1855, and named it after [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]]. The river plunges over a [[Basalt|basalt]] plateau into a chasm, and its spray often rises over 400 m (1,300 ft), visible from up to 50 km (30 mi) away. Flood season peaks in April, when the foot and face of the falls cannot be seen, while in the dry season up to half of the rock face may be exposed. A major tourist destination since the mid-20th century, the falls are listed on the [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] under both names.

Natural harbour in [[Hong Kong|Hong Kong]] separating Hong Kong Island from the Kowloon Peninsula. Its sheltered waters on the [[South China Sea|South China Sea]] helped make Hong Kong a British colony in 1841 and a major trading hub. Originally called Hong Kong Harbour, it was renamed Victoria Harbour to assure shelter for the British fleet under [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]]. Annual fireworks and promenades make it a tourist attraction, and it remains a port for thousands of international vessels each year. Land reclamation on both shores has narrowed the harbour and sparked controversy over water quality and loss of natural habitat.

State in southeastern [[Australia|Australia]], the most densely populated Australian state, with a population of over 7 million. Named for [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]], it was separated from [[New South Wales|New South Wales]] as a Crown colony in 1851 and gained responsible government in 1855. Its capital, [[Melbourne|Melbourne]], was the largest city in Australasia by the time of Federation in 1901, and it was the seat of federal government until [[Canberra|Canberra]] became the national capital in 1927. The Victorian gold rush of the 1850s and 1860s greatly increased the population and wealth of the colony.

Period of [[Queen Victoria|Queen Victoria]]'s reign over the United Kingdom, from 1837 to 1901, when the British Empire was the world's hegemonic superpower. Victorian society valued high standards of personal conduct, which gave impetus to social reform but also restricted some groups. Prosperity rose, and literacy and childhood education became nearly universal in Great Britain, but [[Slum|slum]] housing and disease remained severe. Britain was advanced in industry and engineering. Great Britain's population grew rapidly, while Ireland's fell sharply after the [[Great Famine (Ireland)|Great Famine]] of the mid-1840s.

Wild South American camelid of the high [[Andes|Andes]], a relative of the [[Llama|llama]]. It is believed to be the ancestor of the domesticated [[Alpaca|alpaca]], which is raised for its coat, and [[DNA|DNA]] research published in 2001 demonstrated that alpacas may have vicuña parentage. The vicuña produces very small amounts of extremely fine wool, which is expensive because the animal must be caught from the wild and can be shorn only every three years. The Inca allowed only royalty to wear vicuña garments, and today the vicuña is the national animal of [[Peru|Peru]] and appears on its coat of arms. It was heavily hunted until only about 6,000 animals were left when it was declared endangered in 1974. Its population has since recovered to about 350,000, and it lives at altitudes of 3,200 to 4,800 m (10,500–15,700 ft) in the central Andes.

Optical instrument that captures [[Video|video]], unlike a movie camera, which records images on film. Video cameras were first developed for the [[Television|television]] industry and are now used for [[Surveillance|surveillance]], military and industrial work, and consumer recording. Live feeds show images for immediate viewing, while recorded video has moved from videotape to optical discs, hard disks and flash memory. Electronic camera tubes, including [[Philo Farnsworth|Philo Farnsworth]]'s image dissector, replaced mechanical Nipkow disks by the 1930s and stayed in wide use until the 1980s. Solid-state image sensors, such as the [[Charge-coupled device|charge-coupled device]] and later CMOS sensors, eliminated problems such as image burn-in and made digital video practical. These sensors rest on metal–oxide–semiconductor technology, which originates from the [[MOSFET|MOSFET]], invented at [[Bell Labs|Bell Labs]] in 1959. Modern forms include studio and field cameras, camcorders, pan–tilt–zoom surveillance cameras, webcams and the cameras built into many [[Smartphone|smartphones]].
